title: Purple Nutsedge: How to Spot and Control Mutha in Your Rice Field
metaTitle: Purple Nutsedge in Rice: How to Identify and Control It
metaDescription: Purple nutsedge can cut rice yield by 42 percent. Learn to spot it, why its tubers keep coming back, and how flooding helps you stop it in your palay.
excerpt: Purple nutsedge is a stubborn perennial sedge of irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. Farmers call it barsanga, mutha or sudsud, and its scientific name is Cyperus rotundus. Instead of seed, it spreads through tubers and rhizomes hidden in the soil. This page shows how to spot it and how to control it with timing, water and weeding.

blocks.text: What Is Purple Nutsedge?

This damo is a sedge from the Cyperaceae family. Farmers know it as barsanga, mutha or sudsud. In the past, purple nutsedge was a problem mainly in upland rice areas of the Philippines. Over time it adapted, and now it also infests irrigated and rainfed lowland fields.

It is a perennial, and it spreads through tubers and rhizomes instead of relying on seed. Under the soil it builds a network of a basal bulb, rhizomes, tubers and roots. That network lets it push up many young shoots quickly. So one plant soon becomes a patch, and pulling the leaves alone does not kill it. That is why it is so hard to get rid of. You have to deal with what lies under the soil, not just what you see above it.

blocks.caption: Quick facts about purple nutsedge
rows: Irrigated and rainfed lowland rice fields

blocks.text: How to Identify Purple Nutsedge

Like all sedges, it has a solid, three sided stem with no nodes. The stem stands erect, feels smooth and does not branch. Its leaves are also dark green. At the top of the stem, the flowers sit in red brown spikelets, which give the plant its purple tint. Dig gently around the base and you will find the giveaway, a bulb with rhizomes and small tubers in the soil.

items: Smooth, erect, three sided stems that do not branch.
Dark green leaves growing from the base of the plant.
Flower heads with red brown spikelets at the top of each stem.
Small tubers and a bulb at the base when you dig up a plant.
Many young shoots coming up close together, linked by rhizomes under the soil.
Patches that come back in the same spots after weeding or plowing.

blocks.text: Why It Hurts Your Palay

Purple nutsedge is a C4 plant, and experts consider it the worst weed on the planet. It multiplies fast in the soil, survives harsh conditions and infests many crops. In the Philippines it used to dominate only upland rice areas. Now it has adapted and infests irrigated and rainfed lowlands as well.

In full competition with upland rice, it reduces yield by 42 percent. Even in flooded fields, it still cuts the yield of transplanted rice by 38 percent and wet direct seeded rice by 28 percent. One study suggested controlling it at 14 to 29 days after transplanting for transplanted rice. For wet direct seeded rice, the window is 18 to 26 days after seeding.

blocks.title: Its weak spot
blocks.text: This weed has a few weak points you can use. Its tubers cannot sprout if you plow them under and flood the field at the same time. So plow, then bring in water right away. In wet seeded rice, flooding as early as 7 days after seeding reduces its growth. Nature also helps. A leaf rust caused by Puccinia philippinensis attacks its leaves, and Bactra moth larvae feed on its bulbs.
How to Control Purple Nutsedge

items: Dig out plants with their bulbs, rhizomes and tubers, because any tuber left in the soil can send up new shoots.
Plow the tubers under and flood the field at the same time, since buried tubers cannot sprout that way.
In wet direct seeded rice, bring water into the field as early as 7 days after seeding to slow its growth.
Focus your weeding at 14 to 29 days after transplanting, or 18 to 26 days after wet direct seeding.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Sedges

If water and weeding cannot hold purple nutsedge down, choose an active ingredient that works on sedges at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.title: When a spray stops working
blocks.text: This weed is vulnerable to herbicides such as 2,4 D, MCPA or bispyribac sodium, used at the right rice age and always by the FPA registered label.
Spray Safely

Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Purple Nutsedge Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Plow and harrow well, and rake out the runners, roots or pieces you turn up. A small piece left in wet soil can grow a new plant.
Pull escapes before their flower clusters turn brown, since one clump drops a great deal of tiny seed.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [sedge weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Purple Nutsedge

items.q: What do farmers call purple nutsedge in Tagalog and other local languages?
items.a: Farmers know it as barsanga, mutha or sudsud. Its scientific name is Cyperus rotundus. Note that barsanga is also a local name for haspan flatsedge, so check the base of the plant before you decide. A plant with small tubers in the soil and red brown spikelets on top is most likely this weed.

items.q: How do I kill it in my rice field?
items.a: Combine several steps. Plow the tubers under and flood the field at the same time. In wet seeded rice, flood as early as 7 days after seeding. Dig out escapes with their tubers. If you use a herbicide, choose one that works on sedges and fits your rice age, and always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does it keep coming back after I weed?
items.a: It comes back because the part you see is only the top. Below the soil it keeps a basal bulb, rhizomes, tubers and roots. These let it send up many new shoots quickly. Pulling the leaves alone leaves the tubers behind. So dig out the tubers, and use flooding to keep buried ones from sprouting.
